concepts.example: For a 4096 by 4096 matrix, full adaptation updates 16,777,216 parameters. Rank 8 LoRA trains 8*(4096+4096)=65,536 parameters, about 0.391% of that matrix. This is a per-matrix calculation; embeddings and selected module counts affect the whole model. Seven billion weights at 16 bits occupy an ideal 14 billion bytes. At four bits they occupy an ideal 3.5 billion bytes, before metadata and higher-precision components. Adapter training additionally needs gradients, optimizer states and activations. These numbers explain the opportunity for memory reduction without claiming that a particular GPU can train every seven-billion-parameter model at every sequence length.
concepts.explanation: QLoRA trains LoRA adapters over a frozen, quantized base model. Its design uses four-bit NormalFloat (NF4), double quantization of quantization constants and paged optimizers. NF4 is not simply uniform integer rounding. Computation typically uses a higher precision such as bfloat16 while compressed weights remain frozen. PEFT is the umbrella category; QLoRA is not an alternative to PEFT. Select the target linear modules, rank, scaling, learning rate and data carefully. Increasing rank increases adaptation capacity and optimizer memory, but does not guarantee better generalization. Low-rank updates optimize the downstream training objective, not necessarily reconstruction of the original floating-point weights. Some tasks need different modules or a different adaptation strategy. Compare a baseline, a LoRA run and a quantized-adapter run on the same evaluation set. Measure task quality and general regressions as well as time and memory; there is no universal percentage saving or speedup.
concepts.title: QLoRA & PEFT

concepts.example: Suppose the policy log probabilities for chosen and rejected responses are -2.0 and -3.0, and reference log probabilities are -2.5 and -2.5. The reference-adjusted margin is 1.0. At beta=0.1 the logit is 0.1 and the DPO loss is approximately 0.644397. If policy and reference are identical, the margin is zero and the loss is log(2), approximately 0.693147. Human preference labels identify which response is chosen; subtracting arbitrary human numeric scores is not this DPO objective. A lower pair loss alone does not establish better answers on unseen prompts.
concepts.explanation: Standard DPO uses a prompt, chosen response and rejected response, together with a frozen reference policy. Define d = (log pi(chosen|x)-log pi_ref(chosen|x)) - (log pi(rejected|x)-log pi_ref(rejected|x)). The loss is -log sigmoid(beta*d). Response log probabilities sum the response-token log probabilities with padding and prompt tokens masked appropriately. DPO removes the separate learned reward-model training and online rollout loop of a typical PPO-based RLHF pipeline. It does not eliminate the reference-policy term, data-quality requirements or all stability issues. PPO uses sampled behavior, an advantage estimate and a clipped probability-ratio objective. In RLHF, a learned reward model and a reference-policy KL penalty are common; PPO itself is a general algorithm and does not inherently require a learned reward. DPO suits offline paired preferences. PPO can optimize an online reward process but brings extra rollout, reward and value-estimation complexity. Evaluate either approach for preference overfitting and reward exploitation.
concepts.title: DPO vs PPO Alignment

concepts.example: A seven-billion-weight model has a 14 GB ideal FP16 weight payload and a 3.5 GB ideal four-bit payload, using decimal GB. Actual checkpoint size exceeds or differs from these estimates because of scale metadata, tensor selection and packing. If an application can spend 6 GB on weights, that lower bound suggests exploring four-bit storage; it does not prove the whole serving process fits in 6 GB. First confirm runtime support, then measure checkpoint size, peak memory, prefill latency, decode throughput and held-out quality. Select a precision/runtime combination only after comparing those measurements on the intended workload.
concepts.explanation: AWQ means Activation-aware Weight Quantization. It uses representative activations to guide channel scaling and protect important weights from excessive quantization error while retaining low-bit storage. It is not defined by storing a fixed percentage of large weights in eight bits. GGUF is a model file/container format that can hold metadata and tensors with supported encodings; it is not a competing calibration algorithm. A GGUF file may contain different tensor precisions. Its runtime must understand the architecture and tensor types. Comparing an AWQ checkpoint with a GGUF checkpoint therefore requires specifying model, bit configuration, calibration or conversion procedure, runtime and hardware. Lower bit width saves weight storage, but task accuracy and speed depend on kernels, memory bandwidth, batch size and context length. Do not assume quantized inference is always faster or slower. Re-evaluate converted artifacts rather than transferring an accuracy claim from an unrelated configuration.
concepts.title: AWQ & GGUF Quantization

examples.title: Uniform rounding as a limited toy quantizer
examples.code:
import math
w = [0.12, -0.34, 0.76, -0.22]
s = 0.2
q = [max(-8, min(7, round(x / s))) for x in w]
reconstructed = [s * x for x in q]
squared_error = sum((a-b)**2 for a,b in zip(w,reconstructed))
print(q)
print(round(squared_error, 6), round(math.sqrt(squared_error), 6))
examples.explanation: The integer codes are [1, -2, 4, -1] and the reconstructed values are [0.2, -0.4, 0.8, -0.2]. Squared error is 0.012; its square root is approximately 0.109545. Clamping restricts codes to sixteen possible signed values. Python still stores the list as ordinary integers, so this demonstration does not physically pack four-bit storage. It illustrates scale, rounding, clipping and reconstruction only. It is neither NF4 nor AWQ. A smaller numerical reconstruction error is useful to inspect but does not automatically imply a smaller language-model task error. Evaluate the actual quantized model as well as the arithmetic.

examples.title: Reference-adjusted DPO loss
examples.explanation: This scalar calculation returns 0.644397 using a numerically stable softplus expression. It accepts already computed sequence log probabilities. A training implementation must use differentiable tensor operations, compute the probabilities using the correct tokenizer and response mask, and keep reference-policy parameters frozen. This example uses standard-library math to make the arithmetic independently checkable; it is not an optimizer or a full alignment trainer. If both policy and reference assign identical relative probabilities, the result is log(2). Increasing the chosen-response margin lowers this pair loss, but generalization requires separate evaluation.

flow: 1. Load the base model in a quantized format (e.g., 4-bit NF4) to reduce memory usage. This step is critical for fitting large models on consumer hardware. The quantization format should be chosen based on the available memory and the desired accuracy.

2. Add low-rank adapters (LoRA) to the model. These adapters are small matrices that are trained in higher precision (e.g., 16-bit). The rank of the adapters determines the capacity of the fine-tuning. A higher rank allows for more complex adaptations but increases memory usage.

3. Prepare the dataset for fine-tuning. The dataset should contain input-output pairs for supervised fine-tuning or preference pairs for alignment. The data should be preprocessed to match the model's input format.
4. Train the adapters using a suitable optimizer (e.g., AdamW). The learning rate should be small to avoid overfitting. The training loop should monitor the loss and adjust hyperparameters as needed.

5. Evaluate the fine-tuned model on a validation set. The evaluation should include both task-specific metrics and general language understanding tests. This step ensures that the fine-tuning has not degraded the model's general capabilities.

Choose an adapter-aware serving runtime, or merge using a supported higher-precision workflow and then requantize if needed. Re-evaluate the final artifact; merging is not automatically lossless or memory-free.

7. Deploy the model in a production environment. The deployment should include monitoring for performance and accuracy. The model should be regularly updated with new data to maintain its effectiveness.
foundations:
Separate three decisions: what behavior to teach, which parameters to update, and how to store the resulting model. Supervised fine-tuning uses examples of desired responses. Preference optimization uses comparisons between responses. Neither guarantees factual correctness, so maintain a held-out task evaluation and regression tests for general capabilities. Split data by source or entity where necessary to prevent near-duplicate leakage. A falling training loss is not evidence that deployment quality improved.
A dense matrix W with shape d_out by d_in can receive a low-rank update B A, where B has shape d_out by r and A has shape r by d_in. The trainable parameter count is r(d_out+d_in), rather than d_out*d_in. Scaling by alpha/r controls the update magnitude. This is LoRA, one member of the broader parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) family. Freezing the base weights removes their optimizer states but does not remove forward-pass activations or all gradient computation.
Quantization encodes numerical values using a smaller set of representable values. Storage precision and arithmetic precision differ: weights can be stored at four bits and dequantized into a higher-precision computation. Memory planning must include scales, unquantized layers, adapters, optimizer states, activations and inference KV caches. An ideal weight-only byte count is therefore a lower bound, not a capacity guarantee. Longer sequences and larger batches can exhaust memory even when the compressed checkpoint fits. Benchmark peak allocated memory and quality on representative inputs before choosing a deployment configuration.

interview.answer: The main challenges are balancing accuracy and efficiency, choosing the right quantization format, and tuning the fine-tuning hyperparameters. Quantization can introduce errors, but fine-tuning can compensate for these errors. The choice of quantization format depends on the available memory and the desired accuracy. The fine-tuning hyperparameters, such as learning rate and batch size, must be tuned to avoid overfitting. The model should be evaluated on a validation set to ensure that the fine-tuning has not degraded its general capabilities.

introduction: This chapter explores the foundational techniques of LLM fine-tuning and quantization, focusing on QLoRA, DPO, and AWQ/GGUF. These methods are critical for adapting large language models to specific tasks and deploying them on resource-constrained hardware. Fine-tuning updates the model's weights to improve performance, while quantization reduces the precision of the weights to save memory. The chapter begins with the basics of deep learning and transformer architectures, then progresses to advanced techniques. It covers the tradeoffs between accuracy and efficiency, the choice of quantization formats, and the tuning of fine-tuning hyperparameters. The goal is to provide a comprehensive understanding of these techniques, enabling readers to apply them effectively in practice.

practice.answer: To calculate the memory usage, first determine the number of parameters. For a 7B model, there are 7 billion parameters. In FP16, each parameter is 2 bytes, so the total memory is 14GB. In 4-bit, each parameter is 0.5 bytes, so the total memory is 3.5GB. The reduction is 14GB - 3.5GB = 10.5GB. This is a 75% reduction in memory usage. This calculation assumes that the entire model is quantized to 4-bit. In practice, some weights may be kept in higher precision, so the actual reduction may be slightly less.
practice.question: Calculate the memory usage of a 7B parameter model in FP16 and 4-bit quantization.
Using the applied example, compute the loss when policy and reference log probabilities are identical. Why must a training implementation use tensors?
practice.answer: Both log ratios cancel, so d=0 and the loss is -log(0.5)=0.693147. Standard-library math evaluates a scalar but does not retain an automatic-differentiation graph. A training implementation uses tensor log-probabilities and a stable log-sigmoid or softplus operation so gradients reach the trainable policy parameters. The reference model stays frozen.

practice.question: A team compares an AWQ checkpoint and a GGUF file and declares GGUF more accurate. What information is missing?
practice.answer: The comparison must specify the same underlying model, exact tensor precisions, calibration or conversion, runtime, tokenizer, prompts and evaluation metric. AWQ is a quantization method, whereas GGUF is a container supporting multiple encodings. The file extension alone cannot establish accuracy. Evaluate matching tasks and report both quality and resource measurements.

Split and inspect task data; record a base-model evaluation; load a compatible frozen quantized base; attach LoRA modules; train with measured memory and validation checks; retain the best validated adapter. Save tokenizer, base revision, adapter configuration and evaluation results. Serve the adapter separately when supported. Merging may require dequantizing into a higher-precision model and then requantizing, with additional memory and fresh evaluation; never assume it is a lossless in-place operation.
practice.question: Design a pipeline for fine-tuning a 7B model using QLoRA.

practice.answer: To debug a quantized model, first check the quantization format and the precision of the weights. Ensure that the quantization is applied correctly. Check the inference latency and memory usage. Evaluate the model on a validation set to ensure that the quantization has not degraded its performance. If the performance is degraded, try a higher precision quantization format or adjust the fine-tuning hyperparameters. The key is to balance accuracy and efficiency, ensuring that the quantization does not introduce significant errors.
practice.question: How would you debug a quantized model that is producing incorrect outputs?
A rank-8 adapter is added to a 4096 by 4096 matrix. Calculate its parameter count and explain one speed tradeoff.
practice.answer: The two factors contain 8*4096+4096*8=65,536 parameters, compared with 16,777,216 full-matrix parameters. Separate adapters add operations at inference, while merging can remove those operations but may require higher-precision reconstruction and requantization. Actual latency depends on runtime kernels and batching, so measure rather than assuming a speedup.

summary: Fine-tuning changes behavior, PEFT restricts the trainable parameters, and quantization changes numerical representation. QLoRA combines a frozen quantized base with trainable low-rank adapters. DPO learns from paired preferences using policy-to-reference log ratios, while PPO commonly adds an online sampling and reward-estimation loop. AWQ is activation-aware quantization; GGUF is a container for model metadata and tensors. Keep these categories distinct. Capacity estimates must include more than compressed weights, and speed claims require measurement on the deployment hardware. Use held-out data, inspect failures, version training inputs and compare the final serving artifact against the original baseline. Neither efficient adaptation nor reduced precision guarantees task quality.
